item.title: IDFA 2026 winners: Chinese family portrait takes top prize
item.description:
IDFA 2026 winners: Chinese family portrait takes top prize

November 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Year of the Ghost, a Dutch-Chinese documentary about a filmmaker’s mother and sister after his father’s death, has won the top prize at the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA).

Louis Hothothot’s film won three awards at Thursday’s ceremony at the Eye Filmmuseum. It took best film in the International Competition, which carries a €15,000 prize, as well as best editing and the €5,000 award for best Dutch film.

The festival’s 39th edition runs until Sunday, with 253 films from 80 countries. One of the five documentaries in our preview, You Can See Everything, came second in the audience vote.

These are the films that took the main prizes:

The Year of the Ghost
Hothothot was born in China in 1986 as a second child under the one-child policy and moved to Amsterdam in his twenties. His first film, Four Journeys, opened at IDFA in 2021. In this second film, Covid restrictions stop him from getting back to China in time to say goodbye to his father. He then follows his mother, who wants to stay in her husband’s home town to care for his spirit, and his sister, who is trying to get by as a single woman in a big city. The jury praised the film’s “bold honesty, a rare attention to detail, cinematic curiosity and love”.

Memories of Lightning
Riccardo Giacconi’s French-Italian film won best film in the Envision Competition for experimental work, also worth €15,000. Radio journalist Sibilla Scinti Roger (30) travels to an almost deserted village in Le Marche, central Italy, to make an audio documentary about a murder there in 1982 – and finds out the 14-year-old victim was her aunt. Scinti Roger also won the award for outstanding artistic contribution.

Hazara Town
Afghan-born director Khadim Dai won the award for best first feature and the international critics’ prize (Fipresci), as well as a special mention in the International Competition. The film follows his Hazara family, who fled Afghanistan 20 years ago and now face growing persecution in Pakistan. They have to decide whether to stay together or leave one by one, knowing they may never see each other again.

The Clearing
Dutch director Sabine Groenewegen won the award for best use of archive footage, sponsored by the media archive Beeld & Geluid. Her film is a feminist history of Dutch colonial rubber plantations in the Dutch East Indies, where local women were subjected to violence and sexual enslavement. On the festival’s opening night, Groenewegen also received the €50,000 Cultuurfonds documentary grant, which an anonymous donor gives every year to a Dutch documentary maker.

Women and War
The €5,000 audience award, announced on Friday, went to Elwira Niewiera’s German-Polish-Ukrainian documentary. Four women attend therapy sessions in a chalet in the Ukrainian mountains, each trying to recover from very different traumatic experiences of the war. Festivalgoers gave it an average score of 4.856 out of 5, just ahead of You Can See Everything on 4.842.

Other winners included Joël Akafou’s Lonan Tché for best directing and Tala Hadid’s Bardi, set among horse riders in central Morocco, for best cinematography. Raluca Lupaşcu’s A Modern Roma Fairytale got a special mention for best Dutch film, and Ant Hampton’s Dutch-Belgian All the Downtime won the DocLab award for digital storytelling.

The full list of winners is on the IDFA website.

item.title: Inburgering with DN: understanding education system acronyms
item.description:
Inburgering with DN: understanding education system acronyms

November 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

International parents in the Netherlands often find the Dutch school system baffling: HBO, SBO, DUO, WO… the jargon is endless. So to help you pass this particular parenting test, our Inburgering course this month looks at educational acronyms and the like.

Lesson 65: educational jargon

Primary school in the Netherlands is relatively straightforward – although parents often face a bewildering number of school philosophies when deciding which school to entrust their offspring to. It is in groep 8, the final year of primary school, that the trouble really starts.

Doorstroomtoets
Previously known as the Citotoets and the Eindtoets Basisonderwijs, the doorstroomtoets is taken by children in their final year at primary school. The tests focus on language and arithmetic, and the results are used to help determine which type of secondary education children should go on to. In principle, the teacher’s recommendation takes precedence.

The Dutch love of tests and early streaming has been widely criticised, and more secondary schools now offer mixed-ability classes in the first and second years.

Secondary education itself is divided into three main streams. Schools may offer just one – typically in cities – or a combination.

VWO
VWO (voorbereidend wetenschappelijk onderwijs, or preparatory academic education) is the highest level of Dutch secondary education and is followed by some 20% of pupils. A VWO education takes six years, with pupils choosing a specialism (profiel) in the sciences or humanities after three. There are two variants: atheneum and gymnasium. Gymnasium pupils take Latin and Greek in addition to the dozen or so other VWO subjects.

HAVO
HAVO (hoger algemeen voortgezet onderwijs) literally means ‘higher general continued education’. It takes five years to get a HAVO diploma, which prepares school leavers for a hogeschool (see HBO below) rather than a university. Around 30% of pupils are in a HAVO stream. After three years, HAVO pupils also choose a specialism in the sciences or humanities.

VMBO
VMBO stands for voorbereidend middelbaar beroepsonderwijs (preparatory intermediate vocational education). Some 50% of pupils attend this type of secondary education, which is subdivided into four streams. It takes four years to complete a VMBO course.

The most academic VMBO stream is still widely known as MAVO (middelbaar algemeen voortgezet onderwijs, or intermediate general continued education), after the type of school it replaced in 1999.

Middle-class parents push hard to avoid a VMBO recommendation, hence the popularity of tutors and crammers – and exam stress – for 12-year-olds.

SBO, SO and VSO
Special needs pupils have their own category of jargon, depending on their age, the nature of their disability and how much care they need. The main types are speciaal basisonderwijs (SBO, special primary education), speciaal onderwijs (SO, special education) and voortgezet speciaal onderwijs (VSO, special secondary education).

Lighthouse Special Education in The Hague is the only international school for special needs pupils.

After secondary school, most young people move on to further education. Education is compulsory until 16, and until 18 for anyone who does not yet have at least a HAVO, VWO or MBO level 2 diploma.

MBO
MBO, or middelbaar beroepsonderwijs (vocational education and training), is the highest level of education reached by around 40% of the working population. There are four levels of MBO diploma, and students can either attend college full time or combine work and study.

HBO
There are two types of degree course in the Netherlands: the academic courses offered by universities and the more vocational courses (HBO, or hoger beroepsonderwijs) offered by hogescholen. Their umbrella body, the Vereniging Hogescholen, calls them ‘universities of applied sciences’ in English. The Netherlands has 36 hogescholen ranging from art academies to hotel schools and technical colleges.

WO
The Netherlands has 14 official universities offering wetenschappelijk onderwijs (research-oriented education), including the Open University. Delft, Eindhoven and Twente are universities of technology, while Wageningen focuses on agriculture and food. A bachelor’s degree takes three years, a master’s one or two.

DUO
If you have any connection to post-school education, you cannot avoid dealing with the education ministry’s Dienst Uitvoering Onderwijs (DUO), which runs student finance and related services. DUO holds the diploma records that colleges and universities use to check whether you can enrol, organises the lotteries for popular courses and works out how much student finance you are entitled to.

After you graduate, DUO will follow you for years to make sure you pay back your student loan. DUO should not be confused with DUWO, which specialises in student housing.

item.title: Prosecutors hacked and wiretapped Tata Steel, court hears
item.description:
Prosecutors hacked and wiretapped Tata Steel, court hears

November 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The public prosecution service (OM) hacked into Tata Steel’s internal communication network, wiretapped phones, and made video recordings as part of its investigation into alleged criminal pollution, it was revealed on Friday in Amsterdam’s district court.

During the first hearing of the case, the OM revealed it had conducted a “covert intrusion into Tata Steel’s corporate network”, broadcaster NOS reported. Documents were also taken, witnesses questioned and deposition measurements examined.

The case, which has been years in the making, accuses the steelmaker of intentionally ignoring harmful pollution stemming from its coke and gas plants in IJmuiden.

Police and prosecutors are allowed to use hacking techniques in criminal cases under highly specific circumstances. This has been allowed since 2019, NOS reported, and only in a handful of cases, including child pornography and criminal communication investigations.

A defence lawyer for Tata Steel said that there was “unfounded distrust” against the company, that its employees go to work to do the right thing, and that “wire tapping and hacking” had been used as part of an “unbalanced” criminal file.

The investigation is ongoing and could lead to the prosecution of individual executives of the company. The process is not expected to be completed until the first quarter of next year, the OM said, at which point it will also become clear if the current CEO Hans van den Berg could be charged.

The public health institute RIVM records an above-average rate of lung cancer for residents living around the plant, and soot regularly collects in the surrounding neighbourhoods, including school playgrounds.

Many people have suffered serious health problems, which they attribute to the plant.

In 2021, lawyer Bénédicte Ficq filed a complaint on behalf of 1,200 residents and the following year prosecutors began investigating. In July, the OM summoned Tata Steel to court on criminal charges.

Shortly thereafter, the government said it could pull out of a planned €2 billion subsidy package for the company if the criminal case raises “serious concerns” for the Dutch state.

The coalition parties emerge from a weekend of crisis talks agreeing to ruin Sybrand Buma’s Christmas by asking him to chair reconciliation talks after last week’s budget debacle. To the shock of absolutely nobody, Forum voor Democratie turns out to be infested with neo-Nazis who spend their leisure hours cage fighting and celebrating Hitler’s birthday in the Luxembourg forest. The Netherlands continues to lag behind on disability access and women’s pay, despite making progress in both areas. Dutch weapons manufacturer Destinus claims the credit for destroying part of Vladimir Putin’s flagship bridge to Crimea. A Van Gogh painting that was at the centre of a Nazi-era ownership dispute fetches a record price at auction. And in sport, Oranje go down to one of their worst defeats to old rivals Germany just days after achieving an epic victory against Greece.

item.title: Bruna and Readshop avoid bankruptcy, for now
item.description:
Bruna and Readshop avoid bankruptcy, for now

November 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Audax, the parent company of the popular Bruna and Readshop shops, was granted two months of protection against creditors by a Breda court Thursday.

The move follows a provisional cooling-off period granted to the company earlier this month and a hearing earlier this week attended by more than 10 creditors and auditors, many of whom signaled they were willing to grant Audax more time to get its financial affairs in order.

Audax, which was acquired by Lector Capital in January 2026, has been experiencing financial difficulties for years. It says at the time of the acquisition, Lector agreed to invest €8.6 million in Audax, money they say never came through.

Audax is said to owe its suppliers more than €9 million. Some have demanded payment before delivering new products, which could impact the upcoming Christmas shopping season.

item.title: Exiled Colombian climate activist wins children’s peace prize
item.description:
Exiled Colombian climate activist wins children’s peace prize

November 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A 17-year-old Colombian climate activist, Francisco Javier Vera Manzanares, has won the 2026 International Children’s Peace Prize given out by the Amsterdam-based KidsRights Foundation for “putting children’s rights at the heart of climate justice”.

The young activist is currently living in exile in Spain after receiving death threats over his activism in Colombia.

“Although our 17-year-old winner Francisco is an example of peaceful activism for climate rights defenders around the world, he has been forced to flee due to violent death threats against him,” KidsRights chairman Marc Dullaert told broadcaster NOS.

“It is shocking that peaceful child activists are threatened and that governments are unable to protect these children and their right to be heard.”

But in the imposing Peace Palace in The Hague Thursday afternoon, it was all celebration as Francisco received the prize from 72-year-old Kailash Satyarthi, an Indian child rights activist and 2014 Nobel Peace Prize winner.

“All children around the world have the right to live on a healthy, clean, dignified, and peaceful planet,” Francisco said.

Child activist

Francisco got involved in climate action in 2019 after seeing devastating wildfires engulf the Amazon rainforest. At just nine-years-old, he and six friends founded Guardians for Life, which today has more than 1,400 young members from across Colombia and Latin America.

He became the first child ever in Colombia to speak before Congress that same year.

According to KidsRights, Francisco “believes children are citizens of today, not just tomorrow, and should have a meaningful voice in the decisions that shape their lives and futures.”

He’s served as a Child Advisor to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, helping to craft implementation guidelines on children’s rights and climate change.

Francisco’s work has led to the planting of more than 5,000 trees across Latin America and Europe and the training of some 10,000 young people in climate leadership, human rights and citizen participation.

More young winners

Francisco was chosen from 280 nominations across 57 countries. Former winners include Swedish activist Greta Thunberg, who won the prestigious award in 2019.

Two finalists were also recognised at Thursday’s ceremony, Chilean justice activist Issaiah Guzman Arancibia (15) and 17-year-old Sufaira, a Rohingya refugee from Myanmar currently living in Bangladesh who works to prevent child marriages.

Some 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh refugee camps after a 2017 government crackdown that judges in the same Peace Palace ruled hours before the award ceremony was a genocide committed by Myanmar against its Rohingya population – the first time a country has been held responsible for committing genocide.

item.title: Students walk out against conscription and defence spending
item.description:
Students walk out against conscription and defence spending

November 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

High school and university students nationwide will walk out of their classrooms at 1pm on Friday in a National Peace Protest against conscription and increasing defence spending, part of an international action day also taking place in 24 other countries including Germany, England and France.

“In our opinion, money is being taken away from care, education and housing to go to defence,” National Student Union (LSVb) chairwoman Evy Kras told RTL news. “At the same time, they want us to enlist. Young people feel betrayed and say: so far and no further. We want to be invested in us.”

She says these political spending choices are at the expense of young people, and that campaigns by the defence ministry paint an unrealistic picture of war. “They pretend it’s all very adventurous and flashy, but fighting in a war is not flashy.”

The LSVb, together with research and activist group Stop Wapenhandel, published a report earlier this week saying that defence spends €260 million annually on recruitment campaigns at schools and online. Meanwhile, they say, students have trouble making ends meet.

In at least 16 Dutch cities and dozens of schools, students will leave their classrooms at 1pm, fighting for an “affordable future”. In Amsterdam, students will gather at the Stopera, while in Utrecht, they’ll head to the Domplein and in Groningen to the Broerplein.

The Dutch group Stop the War Fever, which is organising the walkout, says on its website that the government refuses to work towards peace yet “pumps billions into weapons and war.”

Conscription

The group is asking to do away with conscription, move defence out of education and invest in the future of young people instead of weapons of war.

Currently, both men and women in the Netherlands aged between 17 and 45 must register for conscription, but since 1997, there has been no obligation to serve.

But the government is preparing legislation for a selective military conscription system that could be employed if it’s deemed necessary for security reasons.

Junior minister Derk Boswijk said in March that he couldn’t rule out the deployment of young people in the coming years.

“Many young people see it coming, now that the war is near at hand on the European continent,” student Camiel Breet told RTL News. “We want to fight against the cabinet’s plans.”

“This is the first post-Cold War generation that is both the generation of misfortune and grows up with the threat of war,” Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam professor of social change and conflict Jacquelien van Stekelenburg told RTL News. “A basic sense of peace is no longer self-evident for them.”

item.title: Tata Steel goes on trial accused of deliberate air pollution
item.description:
Tata Steel goes on trial accused of deliberate air pollution

November 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The criminal case against Tata Steel over alleged deliberate air pollution around its IJmuiden plant began at Amsterdam district court on Friday.

The public prosecution service (OM) accuses Tata Steel IJmuiden of intentionally and unlawfully releasing harmful substances into the air. The complainants say they suffer serious health problems and worry about local children, with soot accumulating in local playgrounds, broadcaster NOS reported. The public health institute RIVM has recorded above-average lung cancer rates in the area.

The case began in 2021, when lawyer Bénédicte Ficq filed a complaint on behalf of people living near the plant. Prosecutors opened an investigation the following year and announced in July that they would take the company to court. They are still considering whether individual managers can be held personally liable.

The case focuses on the plant’s coke-making ovens, where coal is heated at very high temperatures without oxygen to produce coke, a material used to make steel. If the coal is not heated for long enough, it remains partly unfinished (called raw coke) and can release harmful gases into the air and spread soot into the environment.

Tata says it is technically unavoidable that a batch is sometimes not heated for long enough. Prosecutors suspect the company accepts these incidents and deliberately does not report them. In July, Tata called the allegations “essentially unjust”.

Ficq told NOS it was “a tremendously important day” and said the emissions incidents were “foreseeable and avoidable”. She wants executives, including chairman Hans van den Berg, to be prosecuted as well.

€2bn subsidy at steak
The criminal case also affects a €2 billion state support package for Tata’s switch to greener steel. The cabinet said in July that it could pull out of the deal if the investigation raised “serious concerns”. According to NOS, talks have now been extended to March, and the trial is unlikely to be over by then.

item.title: Jetten “won’t be intimidated” by Russian threats and embassy hit
item.description:
Jetten “won’t be intimidated” by Russian threats and embassy hit

November 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prime minister Rob Jetten has said he will not take “too seriously” a Russian warning that employees of Dutch arms maker Destinus could become legitimate military targets, and said the Netherlands would “not be intimidated” after its embassy in Kyiv was damaged in a Russian attack.

His comments came as Russian president Vladimir Putin vowed revenge for the Crimea bridge attack, in which Destinus says its missiles were used. On Thursday afternoon, the Dutch embassy was damaged during a Russian drone attack on Kyiv. Russia then launched a mass missile attack overnight, killing at least five people in Kyiv and Lviv, according to the Kyiv Independent.

No Dutch embassy staff were hurt and the damage caused to the building was likely indirect, Ukrainian air defence sources told broadcaster NOS. Nevertheless, foreign minister Tom Berendsen has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident.

“Further escalation”
The Russian embassy in the Netherlands released a statement on Thursday evening saying : “it is becoming increasingly difficult to regard the Netherlands as a mere bystander. Through its actions, The Hague is consistently deepening its involvement in the conflict, contributing to its prolongation and further escalation.”

This comes after the admission by Destinus that it was “proudly” involved in striking the Crimea bridge on Tuesday, and revelations in a subsequent investigation by the NRC that showed company personnel had allegedly been actively aiding drone fights on the battlefield with Russia, some of which appeared to be reckless.

The Russian embassy noted these details and pointed to civilian deaths caused by Ukrainian drones, and said that under international law, civilians who take a direct part in hostilities “become legitimate targets”. It also questioned whether the Dutch government was aware of the company’s activities, and demanded “clear explanations”.

The embassy’s claim that at least 40 staff went to Ukraine appears to misread the NRC report, which said it interviewed more than 40 people for the investigation.

❗️Important Statement by the 🇷🇺 Embassy of Russia in the Netherlands.

Have 🇳🇱Dutch defense industry workers become combatants in Ukraine?

Read the full text here:
https://t.co/uNtv0SQ070 https://t.co/Rbl4XQjUq6

— Russian Embassy in NL🇷🇺🇳🇱 (@rusembassynl) November 19, 2026

Jetten responds
Moscow is using the revelations to cover up its own setbacks in the war in Ukraine, Jetten said on Thursday evening during a summit of Ukraine’s allies in Berlin. “If they want to start down that road, we have plenty to say about it too,” he said, referring to Russia’s invasion and the many war crimes it is accused of.

Destinus chief executive Mikhail Kokorich, a former Russian national and Putin opponent, told NRC that staff had launched and operated test drones against Russian drones, but under the direction of Ukrainian soldiers. The company says it does not carry out military operations and only provides technical support under its contracts.

The defence ministry said that using a weapons system against a party to an armed conflict counts as direct participation in hostilities, but giving general instruction on how a system works does not. Civilians who take part directly lose their protection under the laws of war and can be prosecuted.

Defence minister Dilan Yeşilgöz declined to comment on the revelations. The Netherlands helps Ukraine in line with international humanitarian law, “and unfortunately we say nothing about anything else,” she told BNR at an arms fair in Rotterdam on Thursday. It is “much better” to test weapons in an exercise scenario than on a battlefield, she said.

MPs want answers
Defence experts told Nieuwsuur that Yeşilgöz should talk to the company and possibly order an inquiry into its role. That would include a June 2023 test near Kharkiv in which Destinus drones were aimed at targets near the Russian city of Voronezh. A drone hit a home in Voronezh that morning, injuring three people, but NRC could not establish whether it was a Destinus drone.

MPs from coalition and opposition parties have raised concerns. D66’s Mpanzu Bamenga called the report “worrying”, PRO’s Wimar Bolhuis wants explanations about export licences and drone testing, and Volt’s Laurens Dassen has called for an investigation. A senator from PvdD has also tabled written questions, according to NRC.

Foreign trade minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma said Dutch export controls are “very careful”, but that the cabinet has not yet been able to verify everything in the report.

The Dutch state is one of Destinus’ biggest customers. In June the cabinet agreed to pay €250 million for 700 Ruta cruise missiles for Ukraine, a package it first described as drones. After the Crimean bridge strike, which Destinus posted pictures of and said its Ruta missiles were used, Putin ruled out a partial ceasefire and promised a “much more painful” response.

item.title: Over 20,000 new homes completed, government still behind target
item.description:
Over 20,000 new homes completed, government still behind target

November 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Builders completed 18,100 new homes in the Netherlands between July and September, about 3,200 more than in the same period last year, according to figures from national statistics office CBS.

Completions were also up 1,600 compared to the second quarter. Counting conversions of offices and other buildings into homes, as well as demolitions and homes lost to renovation, the housing stock grew by 20,300 homes.

The number of building permits issued for new homes dropped sharply to 16,600, after an unusually high 48,900 in the second quarter. Almost 30,000 of those were issued in June alone. CBS said this was because local authorities rushed to register permits before new rules on grid congestion came into force.

As a result, the number of homes that have permits but have not yet been built fell  by 1,400 to around 257,000. CBS said more homes have been given permits than have been built in recent years.

The value of permitted housing construction was €3 billion in the quarter, 19% lower than a year earlier.

Construction firms’ turnover rose 5.7% year on year, the third quarterly rise in a row. But 163 construction firms went bankrupt in the quarter, 30 more than in the previous three months.

The cabinet wants 100,000 homes to be added each year to tackle the housing shortage. That works out at 25,000 a quarter, around 5,000 more than were added between July and September.
